spec.title: Go scheduler: overview, blueprint and shared contracts

item.title: What the bash belt loses today
Shape: one binary, two processes, one table, one supervised unit
Blueprint: the scheduler in the factory DAG
Domain map: one spec, one package, one owner each
Shared contracts every domain codes against
Status codes and routes rows: who owns what
Build order: waves of disjoint files

spec.purpose: Route an agent to the right scheduler spec in one read, fix the contracts every domain shares, and show where the scheduler sits in the factory DAG. This file defines the shape; each domain spec defines its behaviour.

section.title: What the bash belt loses today
section.text: The line is run by three bash watchers in panes: the route runner applies the routes table, the flow watch calls stalls, the policy watch applies defaults. Each polls a directory, each is serial, none retries.
Lost wakes: a wake is one herdr prompt; when it fails the record becomes a 500 and nothing tries again, and a prompt typed into a seat inside its quiet window is lost with the compaction.
No retry: a seat bring-up refused once (a branch another worktree still holds, a slot not yet back in the pool) is a 500 for ever, though the cause clears a minute later.
False stalls: a gate is called stalled by wall clock alone, so a tester mid-suite reads as a dead line, and a serial bring-up that holds the belt past stale_seconds reads as a stopped belt.
By hand: two watches prompt the architect for every gate record and every finished turn, so the architect is a station of the line instead of its designer, and a dead architect stops tickets.
Owner order: build a lightweight Go scheduler, run it in Podman on WSL, spec every domain in its own XML spec of at most 1000 lines, and put it into the small loop and the factory DAG.
Owner ruling 2026-10-13 02:50Z: SPEC-16 is the engine and the end state of the line. Every bash watcher, patrol and notifier running today is interim glue that a domain here replaces at cut-over.

section.title: Laws the scheduler inherits
section.text: Routing is the table: the scheduler matches a record against the routes table top to bottom and performs the first row. New behaviour is a row, never a branch in Go.
Records, not prose: the scheduler branches on kind, code, attempt and escalations only; a note is for the owner's line and the monitor's screen.

The bus is files in the state root, owned by the scheduler, and routing is by status code through the routes table; NATS is deferred. Intake reads the files through one interface; the gRPC socket is the control plane only.

text.source: ROADMAP.md#Locked decisions; AGENTS.md#Law: runtime data never lives in git; bin/state-root.sh

section.text: Runtime data lives in the state root, never in the repository: records, the routed ledger, jobs, latches and logs. The container mounts the repository read-only and the state root read-write.
The tester, reviewer and merger seats stay and their verdicts are state-root records. The merge and the verify on main are code: after each merge, verified 201 or rejected 422, and no architect wake.
No LLM in routing, health, retry or cleanup: matching, probes, retries and reaping are code. A model seat does ticket work and rulings, and at most explains a finding the code raised.

text.source: node:DEC-no-process-under-agent; AGENTS.md#Law: herdr-first, never background processes

section.text: Every long-running process is a labelled herdr pane: the container runs in one, the executor in one. No shell ampersand, no nohup, no harness background job.
Nothing hardcoded: every tunable is a key in a schema-validated JSON file, variables are resolved at load, a missing key is exit 3 naming the key, and no Go default exists for any of them.

text.source: node:DEC-makefiles-entry-point; AGENTS.md#Law: scope small, integrate in CI

section.text: Make is the entry point: build, test, lint, image, run, status are targets that call scripts, and every build and every test runs in Podman, never on the host.

Pure core, thin edges: matching, planning, retry arithmetic and stall verdicts are pure functions of values; the clock, the file system, the socket and the executor are injected interfaces a test replaces.

text.source: AGENTS.md#Hard rule: dated entry files, one file per entry; events/bin/event.sh; bin/state-root.sh

section.text: One script owns the record format: the scheduler never writes a record file itself, it asks the executor to run the event writer, which writes under the state root, so the log keeps one writer.
The quiet window is honoured: while a seat's quiet file exists, a wake for it is written into that seat's inbox instead of its pane, and the guard drains the inbox after the resume.
Break glass is never automated: the owner grants one command once on the page, the scheduler only runs the seat script with the granted record, and no policy row may ever match a break.glass record.
System before agents: the executor and the scheduler come up in the bring-up chain before any seat, and a seat is refused while the scheduler is down.

section.title: Shape: one binary, two processes, one table, one supervised unit

node.title: The small loop and the factory DAG are scheduled by one lightweight Go service in Podman on WSL, designed domain by domain before it is built
node.text: Owner order: one process replaces the route runner, the flow, policy and two architect watches, from the tables they read. Revised 2026-10-13: the bus is state-root files (C15); SPEC-16 is the engine and the end state.

node.title: The scheduler decides inside a container that holds no host tool and acts only through the executor, a dumb host process behind gRPC on a unix socket; the socket is the control plane and stays
node.text: Rejected: the home directory mounted, typing into a shell pane, the scheduler on the host. Cost: two processes, two panes, one socket. Revised 2026-10-13 (C15): the socket is the control plane, never the bus, and stays.

node.title: scheduler/: a Go service in a Podman container that reads the records of the state root, applies the routes and policies tables, runs every action as a retried job through the host executor, confirms wakes, calls stalls on two signals
node.text: One module, one binary: run, exec, status, parity, check. It mounts the repository read-only and the state root read-write, acts only through the executor socket, and runs every domain loop under one supervised unit.

node.title: scheduler exec: the host half, a gRPC server on a unix socket in a labelled herdr pane that runs an allowlisted verb table (herdr, the seat script, the queue script, the event writer) with a timeout and returns exit code and output tails
node.text: It decides nothing: a verb not in its table is refused, an argument with a newline is refused, every call is one JSON log line. Its socket is the control plane and stays whatever the bus becomes (card C15).

node.title: scheduler.v1 gRPC over unix sockets: Executor.Run(verb, args, idempotency key, timeout) and Executor.Health; Scheduler.Health, Status, Reload and Drain
scheduler/RUNBOOK.md: build and test in Podman, bring the executor pane and the container pane up, read status, switch the mode between off, shadow and active, roll back, and read the parity report

section.text: Two planes. Data: record files in the state root, read by intake. Control: one gRPC socket from the scheduler to the executor for actions, one from the operator to the scheduler for status, reload and drain.

One supervised unit: the domain loops run as goroutines of the one binary under one systemd user unit. No reconciler, watcher or probe gets its own unit, process or pane; the executor is the binary's exec subcommand.

One loop. Each tick: intake lists new records, routing turns each into a plan, the plan becomes jobs, the job runner sends due jobs to the executor, confirmation and health judge what came back, observe reports. Ticks never block on a job.

One state root, small files: the routed ledger (the bash runner's words, so cut-over adopts it), one file per job, the latches, the belt file, the shadow decisions. Nothing in a database, nothing in git.

section.title: Blueprint: the scheduler in the factory DAG
section.text: The SDLC DAG is unchanged: every edge is still a record kind in the routes table. The scheduler is the orchestrator's runner, the thing that moves a record along its edge; seats, gates and the owner's line stay where they are.

section.text: The domains form their own DAG: config feeds everything, intake feeds routing, policies and health, routing feeds jobs, jobs feed the executor client, confirmation and health read what came back, observe reads all of it.

section.text: In the bring-up chain the executor pane and the scheduler pane take the belt's place: herdr, guard, monitors grid, executor, scheduler, then seats. The one supervised unit keeps the binary up as the belt is kept up today.

section.title: Domain map: one spec, one package, one owner each
section.text: One spec per domain, under 1000 lines, one Go package per domain, one build ticket per package. Two tickets that run at once never touch one file; a package is the unit of ownership.

A intake: SPEC-16.A, package intake. The records tree of the state root, ordering by file name, the routed ledger and its claim, the first-start boundary, interrupted claims, validation, the record reader.
B routing: SPEC-16.B, package routes. The routes table loaded and matched, the plan for a record, the receipt, no-route, ignore, and the rows this domain owns.
C seats: SPEC-16.C, package seat. Seat names from role labels, caps and holding, bring-up and down through the executor, status observation, leases, the shared merger seat.
D jobs, retries and confirmation: SPEC-16.D, package job. The job store, backoff, idempotency, dead letter, wake confirmation, the quiet window hold, attempt and escalation rows.
E policies and break glass: SPEC-16.E, package policy. Deadlines, defaults, limits per ticket, the policy.applied record, the break glass lifecycle rows.
F health and supervision: SPEC-16.F, package health. The belt heartbeat, two-signal stalls, latches, the halt flag, graceful drain, recovery on start, the 5xx rows.
G config and schema: SPEC-16.G, package config. scheduler.json and executor.json with their schemas, variable resolution, validation at start, hot reload of the tables.
H Podman runtime and the executor: SPEC-16.H, packages executor and the api proto. The Containerfile, the run contract, the host pane, the verb table, the gRPC services, the one systemd user unit.
I observability: SPEC-16.I, package observe. Structured log lines, the status answer, counters, the record id as the trace id, what the board and the monitor read.
J cut-over: SPEC-16.J, package cutover. The mode flag, shadow mode and the parity report, going active, rollback, retiring the five bash watchers, the acceptance run.
K testing: SPEC-16.K, package testkit and the replay fixtures. The test pyramid, the fake executor, golden replay cases per routes row, the contract test against the event writer, CI.

section.title: Shared contracts every domain codes against
section.text: These types and interfaces live in one package, core, written by the skeleton ticket before any domain package. A domain that needs a field not here raises a question; it never edits core in its own ticket.
Record is a state-root record file as written, plus where it was seen. Optional fields are pointers or zero values; attempt defaults to 1 when absent, exactly as the bash runner reads it.
section.field: UTC stamp, code and five-character suffix, the trace id of every log line about it. The file name, UTC second then a descriptive name, is the sort key.
When it was written; deadlines and stalls are measured from here, never from the file's mtime.
The seat that wrote it; a record whose seat is the scheduler's own seat is never routed.
One of the kinds the event schema allows; the scheduler matches it as a string and never enumerates it in Go.
The work order id, or empty; rows that seat, enqueue or down need one.
The addressee role of a routed or escalated record.
A seat's try count on one ticket, 1 to 3.
The pull request head and number a row that says with pr copies onto the wake line.
Break glass and policy fields, carried through, never interpreted outside their domains.
Prose for humans; no domain branches on it.
The records tree it was first seen in and its path there; scheduler-side only, never written back.
section.text: Row is one entry of the routes table, kept exactly as the schema allows it, with its index in the table and its canonical match string as its identity.
section.field: Position in the table; the first matching index wins.

field.name: Row.Match
field.type: struct of optional ints and strings

section.field: kind, code, code_gte, attempt, attempt_lt, escalations, escalations_lt; an absent key matches anything.

field.name: Row.Do, Row.To, Row.With, Row.Down, Row.Code, Row.Line, Row.PriorityFrom
field.type: string, string, string, string, int, string, string

section.field: The action and its parameters, as named in the schema.
section.text: Plan is what routing decides for one record: pure data, no side effect, so shadow mode can write it down and the parity report can compare it.
section.field: Verdict is one of routed, ignored, unrouted, own, unreadable.
In order: the primary action, then the down, then the receipt. An ignored or own record has none.
section.text: Job is one side effect to perform through the executor, durable in the state root, identified by its key so a restart never performs it twice.
section.field: record id, colon, action, colon, target; the idempotency key and the file name.
The executor verb and its positional arguments; never a shell line.
What the job is about, for the log and for confirmation.
The retry arithmetic's inputs and output.
pending, held, running, confirming, done, dead.
Why it is held (quiet, cap, order), and what the last run said.
Keys of jobs that must reach done or dead first: the down after the primary, the receipt after both.
section.text: Verdict is the executor's answer to one Run, carried unchanged from the proto message.
section.field: Refused means the executor did not run the verb (not in its table, bad argument); Refusal says why.
The last lines, bounded by the executor's config, for the log and the 500 note.
section.text: Seat is what the scheduler knows about one seat from the executor's observation verbs.
section.field: The name is the role label with the ticket lowercased, as the seat script names it.
absent, idle, busy, unknown; Since is when the status was first observed.
section.text: Interfaces, so every domain is testable with fakes: Source, Ledger, Executor, Clock, Table, JobStore, SeatObserver, Latches. The engine wires the real ones; tests wire testkit's.
section.field: List(sinceID) returns new record references across every root in id order; Read(ref) returns the Record or an error that says unreadable.
Claim(id) reports whether this call won the claim; Set(id, word); Get(id); Interrupted() lists ids still claimed at start.
Run(ctx, Job) Verdict; Health(ctx) error. The gRPC client implements it; testkit's fake records every call and answers from a script.
Now() time.Time in UTC; tests set it; nothing calls the system clock directly.
Match(Record, escalations) returns the first Row or none; Rows() lists them; Version() names the loaded file's hash.
Put, Get, Due(now), ByRecord(id), ByState; one file per job under the state root.
Observe(ctx) returns every seat the executor can see with its status, in one call per tick.
Take(name) reports whether the latch was free; Drop(name); a latch is a file so it survives a restart.

section.title: Status codes and routes rows: who owns what
section.text: Every row of the routes table and every status code in the check config is owned by exactly one domain spec, declared there with owns-route or owns-code; the check script proves it and fails the set on a gap or a double.

Codes: 100 and 300 to intake and routing (A, B); 200, 201, 409 to routing (B); 422, 423 to jobs (D); 204 and 400 to policies and break glass (E); 412, 429, 500 to health and seats (F, C). The domain specs carry the declarations.
Rows: the SDLC edges and the ignore rows to routing (B); the attempt and escalation rows to jobs (D); the break glass and policy rows to policies (E); the 5xx rows to health (F).

section.title: Build order: waves of disjoint files
section.text: Owner ruling 2026-10-13 03:00Z: the SPEC-16 files land one pull request each, this overview first, then A to K. The fourteen build tickets cut from the first draft are re-cut only after the owner accepts the revised specs.

text.source: owner:bearings:2026-10-13T03:02Z; AGENTS.md#Law: scope small, integrate in CI

section.text: A build ticket is small: one concern, at most five files and about three hundred lines. A package bigger than that is split into tickets that each own their own files.

text.source: owner:bearings:2026-10-12T18:34Z; AGENTS.md#Law: scope small, integrate in CI

section.text: Four workers build in waves. Inside a wave every ticket owns its own directories and files; a wave starts only when the wave before it is merged, because its packages import the earlier ones.

Wave 0, no shared Go yet: the skeleton (module, pinned dependencies, Makefile, Containerfile, core, testkit, proto and generated code, subcommand registry); the config files and schemas; the replay fixtures; the host files and runbook.
Wave 1, leaves on core: intake (A), routes (B), config loader (G), executor server and client (H).
Wave 2, on wave 1: seats (C), jobs and confirmation (D), policies and break glass (E), health (F).

Wave 3, on everything: the engine and the run subcommand, observe and the status subcommand (I), cut-over and parity (J), the end-to-end acceptance in a scratch herdr session and the lint and CI wiring.
Subcommands register from their own file in the cli package at init, so a wave adds a file and edits none: the skeleton owns the registry and main, each domain owns its subcommand file.

The skeleton pins every dependency the whole module will need, so no later ticket touches the module file; a dependency a later ticket needs that is not pinned is a question to the architect, not an edit.

section.title: Rules every scheduler spec obeys
section.text: Valid against the scheduler spec schema: contents first, every section listed in order, every element that carries words carries a source, graph nodes declared with their sources.
No home path, host, URL, page key, email, ticket id, record id, pane id or em dash anywhere: a spec that ports to another host names only repo-relative files and config variables.
Under 1000 lines, every element under 240 characters of its own words; a domain that needs more is two domains.
Every node a spec declares exists in the graph with the same title; the graph is the source and the spec cites it.
No prose addressed to another agent: a spec speaks in definitions, rules and examples to whoever reads it.

example.text: A new failure class: one row in the routes table, one replay case, make lint. No Go changes.
example.why: The table is the behaviour; Go only applies it.

example.text: A tester wake that herdr refused at 18:31 is retried at 18:31:10, 18:31:30 and 18:32:10, succeeds on the third try after the seat came up, and is confirmed by the tester's work.started record.
A tester mid-suite for twelve minutes is busy in its pane; no stall is called although the gate deadline passed.
Shadow mode ran beside the bash belt for 200 records with zero plan mismatches; the operator flips the mode to active and stops the three watcher panes.
A branch in Go that reads a record's kind to decide what to do with it.
example.why: That is a row that does not exist yet.

example.text: The scheduler container with the home directory mounted so it can run the seat script itself.
example.why: Every host tool version is then bound into the container, and the container is a shell with extra steps.

example.text: A policy row whose match is a break.glass record.
example.why: The owner grants every break glass by hand, once.

example.text: A pull request merges; the verify on main runs as a job, posts verified 201, and the next merge goes ahead with no architect prompt.
example.why: The merge and the verify are code.

example.text: A stall watch in its own systemd unit or pane beside the scheduler.
example.why: Every domain loop runs in the one binary under one supervised unit.

example.text: A health probe that asks a model whether a seat is stuck.
example.why: Probes are code; a model at most explains a finding the code raised.

example.text: A record, ledger line or job file committed to the repository.
example.why: Runtime data lives in the state root.

example.text: A Go function that writes a record file into the log.
example.why: The event writer is the one writer; the executor runs it.
